hilfe: The wiki: explained examples that play themselves.
A page shows a piece of code. Explanations run in one after another: a part
of the code gets framed, a line grows out of the frame to a speech bubble,
the bubble fades in, stays, and goes again. Then the next step comes. At the
end it starts over.
kategorien   The big cards on the start page.
schluessel  this is what the category is called in a page's "kategorie".
name        what the card says.
zeichen     one to three characters for the card, like the tags on the
skill tree nodes. Empty = the first letter of the name.
text        a few words about it. Also shown on the right as long as no
page has been picked.
One category is different: "erze". Its pages are NOT in this file, they
come into being while you play - one per ore that has been in your bag,
plus every processing step you have done with it. So do not write any
"seiten" for it, they would never show up. Name and text of the card do
still come from here.
seiten       One entry = one page in the list on the left.
kategorie   the key from above.
titel       how it appears in the list.
kurz        one sentence below the title.
braucht     the key of a skill tree point - the same ones as in
data/skills.txt: mine, care, sell, bag, check, print, shared, while,
if, else, for, variables, classes, functions, wash, smelt,
cast, clean, polish, harden, refine, press, alloy.
If the point is not bought, the page does NOT show up at all.
Without "braucht" the page is always there.
schritte    the frames of the animation, in order.
One step in "schritte":
punkt      the label on the timeline below. Together the labels are the
table of contents of the animation - you can click them and
jump straight there.
code       the code that is shown. Line break as \n.
It stays in force until a step brings a NEW code. When it
changes, exactly the new characters type themselves in.
The first step of a page needs a code.
markiere   a piece of text FROM THE CODE. It is searched for there and
framed. If it is not found, that shows up in red in the game -
better a message than an animation that does nothing.
treffer    if the piece occurs more than once: which one is meant.
Without it, the first one.
text       what the speech bubble says. Short sentences, no jargon without
explanation - a child should understand this.
dauer      seconds the step stays. Below 1.2 is not allowed, otherwise the
bubble would be gone before it arrived.
The code does not have to be C++. On the pages under "Game" there are small
tables instead - the font is a typewriter font, so everything lines up.
The numbers in the texts come from data/erze.json, data/verarbeitung.json,
data/legierungen.json and data/runden.json. If you change something there,
it belongs updated here.
siehe_auch   list of titles of other pages. They stand on the right as small
links and jump straight there - even into another category.
Only what is already unlocked is shown.
braucht      a key like "check" - or a list of them. With a list ONE is
enough: the page shows up as soon as you have bought any of
them. Without braucht it is always there.
A STEP may have a "braucht" too - but there ALL the named
points have to be bought. The difference has a reason: a page
is a topic, a step is a piece of code, and every single command
in it has to be allowed. Steps that would show something you
could not buy yet simply drop out - together with their mark on
the timeline. That way the wiki never shows a command you are
not allowed to write anywhere.
unter        title of another page. This page then sits indented below it in
the list on the left, and the parent can be folded away. That is
how the eight processing commands hang under the overview
instead of filling half the list.
This works over any number of levels: "item.wash(...)" hangs
under "Processing - overview", and that one under "item".
Only going in a circle is not allowed - the game reports that
and hangs the page back at the top.
At the very top there are exactly two overview points: "block"
is the stone outside (mining, checking), "item" is your bag
(selling, processing, alloying). A new command belongs under
whichever one it fits, using "unter".

kategorien.name: Functions
kategorien.text: Commands you give the game. Every one of them stands in your code, and your robot carries it out. Everything here has to be bought in the skill tree first.

kategorien.name: Control structures
kategorien.text: This is how your program decides and repeats: if, else, while, for, variables, your own functions and classes. That is real C++.

kategorien.name: Ores
kategorien.text: Your collection. Every ore you have mined once gets a page here - and every way you have taken with it gets a row with its price. What you have never done shows up as a ?.

kategorien.name: Game
kategorien.text: How the game itself works: which ores exist, what states and purity mean, how alloying, the bag, the rounds and the skill tree work.

seiten.kurz: The block out there: mining and checking.

schritte.text: Almost every command starts with a name. block is the one stone lying in front of you - everything that has to do with IT starts this way.
mine means to mine it. Nothing more happens out there: the stone then goes into your bag, and that is where it continues.
The second thing block can do: check whether one is there at all. It regrows, so now and then it is gone for a moment.
Both together: only mine when there is something there. That is how almost every program starts.
With while this runs the whole round through, without you doing anything.

seiten.kurz: Your bag: selling, checking, processing.

schritte.text: Once something is mined it no longer belongs to the block but to you. That is why everything about your bag starts with item.
sell sells what is in the bag. Only here is there money - nobody gets rich from mining alone.
has only looks, without taking anything out. That way you sell exactly what you have enough of.
Selling raw brings little. Washing, smelting, polishing, alloying - all these steps work in the bag, never on the block.

seiten.kurz: Mines the block in front of you.

schritte.text: block is the block in front of you. mine means to mine it. This line says: give it one hit.
Every command ends with a semicolon. It says: done, next one please.
One line mines one block. With while you do it again and again, the whole round long.
Every mined block goes into your bag. It only turns into money when you sell it.

seiten.kurz: Valuable blocks want to be cooled or heated first.

schritte.text: The more a block is worth, the more often it wants something: cooling or heating. It always comes out equally fast - but untreated it comes out dirty, and purity is what it is worth.
Asks: does this block want to be cooled? The answer is true or false. Heat is the other one, and Plain means it wants nothing at all.
Into the brackets of mine goes what you do to it. Done right, the block keeps its full purity.
No treatment costs 25 points of purity, the wrong one 50 - heating what wants cooling is worse than doing nothing. So never treat blindly: ask first, every time.
Which one it is changes with every block that regrows. That is why the question belongs inside the loop and not in front of it.
It says over the block what it wants, and every ore page in the wiki says how often that ore asks for it and what it costs you. Cheap ores like stone never ask.

seiten.kurz: Asks whether the block is there right now.

schritte.text: Asks the game: is the block there right now?
The answer is true or false - yes or no. Nothing else ever comes out.
With if your program decides for itself: it only mines when the block is there.
else means otherwise. If the block happens to be gone, your program does something else.
isLoading() is the opposite question: is the block regrowing right now? Both exist so that you do not have to think backwards.

seiten.kurz: Turns your bag into money.

schritte.text: Sells everything in your bag. You get money for it.
Into the brackets you write an ore name - plain, without quotation marks. Then only that kind goes over the counter, your gold stays put.
Any stands for every ore at once. item.sell(Any) is the same as item.sell() - everything goes.
The number says how many pieces. Here exactly three stones, the rest stays in the bag.
sell gives you back how much money there was. You can remember that and look at it.
Raw, a block is worth little. Washed, pressed or polished it brings many times as much. Better sell afterwards.

seiten.kurz: Looks into the bag without selling anything.

schritte.text: Asks: is there at least one stone in my bag? The answer is yes or no. The ore name stands there plainly - no quotation marks.
Any means every ore at once: is there anything at all in my bag? With a number too - item.has(Any, 20) asks for twenty pieces, whatever they are.
With a number you ask for at least that many. Here: do I have ten stones or more?
That way you only sell once something has piled up - and not every single stone right away.
The same before processing: only one job runs at a time, and it costs time. Five at once pays off more than one five times.

seiten.kurz: Writes something into your console.

schritte.text: Writes the text at the bottom of your console. It changes nothing in the game - it is just for you.
Instead of text you may also write a number in there.
That is how you see what is inside a variable. That is exactly what print is for: understanding what your program is doing.
If your program does not run as expected, put a print in. If the text does not appear, your program never gets there either.

seiten.kurz: A note that every console can read.

schritte.text: shared is a note with compartments. Into the compartment points you put the number 10.
+= 1 means: one more. 10 becomes 11, without you having to know the old number.
That is how you get the number back out. It stays in the compartment until you change it.
The note belongs to all consoles together. One writes, another reads - that is how your programs talk to each other.

seiten.kurz: Turning one state into a better one.

schritte.text: Fresh out of the ground a block is raw. Sold like that it brings the very least.
Smelting turns raw copper into smelted copper. Smelted is worth twice as much as raw.
Every step makes the block worth more: polished brings four and a half times as much as raw. But every step costs time too.
Not every command fits every ore. Stone can be pressed but not smelted. The bag shows you what works right now.
There is not just one way. Cleaning, for example, works from raw, washed, cast and pressed. And: only one job runs at a time, the next one has to wait.

seiten.kurz: Washing: raw becomes washed.

schritte.text: Washes all the raw copper in your bag. Washed is worth 1.2 times as much as raw.
With a number you wash exactly that many pieces. Without a number it takes everything that fits.
Washing lifts the purity by 10 points, and it only takes 0.6 seconds per piece. But it only works from raw.

seiten.kurz: Smelting: into the furnace with it.

schritte.text: Melts copper in the furnace. Smelted is worth twice as much as raw - but the purity drops by 5 points.
Smelting works from raw, washed and pressed. With a number you take only that many pieces - that takes 1.5 seconds each.
From smelted comes cast, hardened or alloyed. Casting only works from smelted - that is why the furnace comes first.

seiten.kurz: Casting: liquid metal into a mould.

schritte.text: Pours smelted copper into a mould. Cast is worth 2.8 times as much as raw.
Casting only works from smelted. Without the furnace first nothing happens at all.
From cast it goes on to polished, hardened or cleaned. Casting leaves the purity unchanged.

seiten.kurz: Cleaning: the big jump in purity.

schritte.text: Cleaning gets the dirt out: the purity rises by 18 points. Only refining does more.
It works from four states: raw, washed, cast and pressed. So you can clean almost any time.
Cleaned is worth 2.4 times as much as raw - and from there it goes straight to refining, the most expensive state.

seiten.kurz: Polishing: until it shines.

schritte.text: Polishes a block until it shines. Polished is worth 4.5 times as much as raw.
Polishing works from cast, cleaned and hardened. You cannot polish a raw block.
So clean first, then polish. The purity rises by another 8 points in the process.

seiten.kurz: Hardening: making it hard in the fire.

schritte.text: Hardens iron in the fire. Hardened is worth 3.4 times as much as raw, the purity drops by 4 points.
Hardening works from smelted, cast, pressed and cleaned. And not every ore can do it: gold, for example, cannot.
From hardened it goes on to polished or refined. That is how you get iron all the way to the top.

seiten.kurz: Refining: the last and best step.

schritte.text: Refining is the last step. Refined is worth six times as much as raw - there is nothing above it.
It only works from cleaned, hardened or polished. You cannot refine raw gold.
Clean first, then refine. Refining takes 3 seconds per piece - the slowest step. In return the purity rises by 25 points.

seiten.kurz: Pressing: cheap becomes useful.

schritte.text: Presses stone together. Pressed is worth 1.8 times as much as raw.
Pressing works from raw, washed and cleaned. For cheap ores like stone it is the fastest profit.
Pressing drops the purity by 3 points. So wash first - that brings 10 points and makes up for it.

seiten.kurz: Two ores become a new material.

schritte.text: Makes one piece of bronze. Bronze does not lie in the ground - it only comes into being here.
Bronze needs 2 copper and 1 iron. Both have to be smelted, raw does not work.
So both ingredients into the furnace first, then alloy. Only one job runs at a time - one after the other.
The number says how many pieces you want to make. Without a number it makes exactly one.
An alloy can itself be an ingredient: Electrum and Silver make White Gold. Gold alone is worth 70, White Gold 360.

seiten.kurz: Asks beforehand whether the ingredients are enough.

schritte.text: Asks: how many pieces of bronze could I make right now? The answer is a number.
0 means: not enough. Any other number means yes. That is why the question fits straight into an if.
If it is not enough, you simply smelt some more. That way your program does not wait, it keeps working.
You can also remember the number and make exactly as many pieces as are possible right now.

seiten.kurz: Repeats something as long as the answer is yes.

schritte.text: This line mines one block. One. Then your program is finished.
while means as long as. In the brackets stands true, and true means always true. So it never stops.
Between the curly braces stands what gets repeated. That is called the body of the loop.
Instead of true any question may stand there. Here: keep going as long as the block is there. Once it is gone, the loop stops.
A loop spins very fast. If nothing in it costs time, your program just runs in circles. Always put a command inside.

seiten.kurz: Repeats something a fixed number of times.

schritte.text: for means for. In the brackets stand three things, separated by semicolons.
i is a counter and starts at 0. It remembers how often the loop has already run.
As long as i is smaller than 10 it keeps going. So ten times: 0, 1, 2 and so on up to 9.
i++ means: one more. Without it i would stay 0 forever and the loop would never stop.
That is how you mine exactly ten blocks and sell afterwards. With while you would have to count yourself.

seiten.kurz: Decides whether something is done.

schritte.text: if means if. In the brackets stands a question that only knows yes or no.
Only if the answer is yes is this done. Otherwise your program skips everything between the braces.
You can also do maths: > is greater, < is smaller, == is equal. Careful, comparing uses two equals signs.
&& means and: both have to be true. || means or - then one of the two is enough.

seiten.kurz: What happens when the answer was no.

schritte.text: If the block is there, it gets mined. If it is gone, your program does nothing at all.
else means otherwise. This part runs exactly when the answer was no.
Either one or the other. Never both, never neither. That way your robot uses the waiting time too, until the block regrows.
else if attaches one more question. It is only asked if the first one was no.

seiten.kurz: A little box where you remember something.

schritte.text: int means whole number. money is the name of the box. 0 is what is in it at the start.
You pick the name yourself. Take one that says what is inside - then you will still understand your code tomorrow.
A single equals sign means: put this in here. Whatever was in there before is gone.
The right side is calculated, the left side gets it put back in. 5 becomes 15. Shorter: money += 10;
int for whole numbers, float for decimals, bool for yes and no. You state the kind when you create it.

seiten.kurz: Your own command, built by you.

schritte.text: main is the function where your program starts. It is always there and does not count.
void means: gives nothing back. mineBlock is the name you pick yourself. The brackets belong to it.
Look where main is: right at the bottom. C++ reads from top to bottom and only ever knows what it has already read. So your functions have to stand ABOVE main.

schritte.punkt: The other way round does not work
schritte.text: Not like this: at this point C++ has never seen the word mineBlock. It complains "is not known here yet" - just swap the two parts around.
That is how you call it: the name with brackets. Then everything you wrote up there runs.
Into the brackets you can pass something in. When calling it you say the number.
Write it once, use it often. And if you want to change something, you change it in one single place.

seiten.kurz: A thing you build yourself, with its own boxes and commands.

schritte.text: struct means blueprint. Counter is the name. Behind it stands everything such a thing has.
value is a box that belongs to every Counter. Every thing has its own.

schritte.punkt: Making a thing out of it
schritte.text: The blueprint alone does nothing. Only here does a counter really come into being, and it is called c.
The dot means: the box value of c. Exactly like block.mine() - block is just such a thing too.
You may write commands into the blueprint too. c.up() then counts one up - the command knows the box value by itself.

seiten.kurz: What is in the ground and how you recognise it.

schritte.code:
Stone      from level 1     value 1
Coal       from level 1     value 3
Granite    from level 2     value 5
Copper     from level 2     value 8
Iron       from level 3     value 14
Silver     from level 5     value 30
Gold       from level 7     value 70
Emerald    from level 10    value 160
Diamond    from level 13    value 400
schritte.text: These are all the ores that occur in the ground. The value says what a raw block brings.
At the start there is only Stone and Coal. The higher your level, the more kinds come along - Diamond only from level 13.
A diamond is worth 400 times as much as a stone. In return it occurs 150 times more rarely and takes 3.5 seconds to mine.

schritte.code:
Stone     grey           Coal      almost black
Granite   pink-brown     Copper    orange
Iron      light beige    Silver    almost white
Gold      yellow         Emerald   green
Diamond   light blue
schritte.text: There is no name on the block. You recognise it by colour and pattern: gold is always speckled yellow, coal almost black.

schritte.punkt: Not every one can do everything
schritte.code:
Stone     raw washed cleaned polished pressed
Copper    raw washed smelted cast ...
Diamond   raw washed cleaned polished hardened
schritte.text: Every ore allows only certain states. Stone can be pressed but not smelted. And you do not melt a diamond either.

schritte.code:
item.has(Stone)          the ore is called Stone
item.has(WhiteGold)      "White Gold" - written together
item.has(Any)            no matter which one

item.has("Stone")        works too, but nothing checks it
schritte.text: Ores stand in your code without quotation marks. They are not text but names the game knows - so a typo is caught right away instead of quietly counting as zero.
Later the game invents ores of its own, and those have names of several words. In code they are written together, without the spaces. Every ore page says at the top what its name looks like there.
Any stands for all ores at once. item.has(Any) asks whether there is anything at all in your bag, item.sell(Any) sells the lot.

seiten.kurz: Two numbers decide what a block is worth.

schritte.code:
raw          factor 1.0
washed       factor 1.2
pressed      factor 1.8
smelted      factor 2.0
cleaned      factor 2.4
cast         factor 2.8
hardened     factor 3.4
polished     factor 4.5
alloyed      factor 5.0
refined      factor 6.0
oxidized     factor 0.6
schritte.text: Every state has a factor. Refined brings six times as much as raw - oxidized even less than raw.

schritte.code:
wash      from: raw
press     from: raw, washed, cleaned
clean     from: raw, washed, cast, pressed
smelt     from: raw, washed, pressed
cast      from: smelted
harden    from: smelted, cast, pressed, cleaned
polish    from: cast, cleaned, hardened
refine    from: cleaned, hardened, polished
schritte.text: This is not a fixed chain but a net: several ways lead out of one state. Only casting works exclusively from smelted.

schritte.code:
purity 0%      price times 0.5
purity 50%     price times 1.0
purity 100%    price times 1.5
schritte.text: Every block also has a purity in percent. A perfectly pure block brings three times as much as a filthy one.

schritte.code:
refine    +25      press     -3
clean     +18      harden    -4
wash      +10      smelt     -5
polish     +8      cast       0
schritte.text: Some steps make the block cleaner, others dirtier. Smelting costs 5 points of purity, refining brings 25.

schritte.code: price = value x state x purity x money per block
schritte.text: This is how the game calculates: the base value of the ore, times the state, times the purity, times the money per block from the skill tree.

seiten.kurz: Two ores become a new material.

schritte.code:
Bronze        2 Copper   + 1 Iron      value 48
Electrum      1 Gold     + 1 Silver    value 165
White Gold    1 Electrum + 2 Silver    value 360
schritte.text: Two different ores become a new material. It is worth more than its parts together.
The ingredients have to be smelted. The recipe does not take them raw - alloying is the last step, not the first.
A new material can itself be an ingredient: Electrum and Silver make White Gold. Gold alone is worth 70, White Gold 360.

schritte.code:
Copper     alloyable with Iron, Silver, Gold
Iron       alloyable with Copper, Silver
Silver     alloyable with Gold, Copper, Iron, Electrum
Gold       alloyable with Silver, Copper
Diamond    alloyable with nothing
schritte.text: Not everything fits together. Stone, Coal, Granite, Emerald and Diamond cannot be alloyed at all.
Afterwards there is a stack of its own in the bag, with its own name and its own colour. You can sell it like any ore.

seiten.kurz: Where your ore sits and how it turns into money.

schritte.code:
Copper   raw          12 pcs   purity 60%
Copper   smelted       4 pcs   purity 55%
Gold     raw           1 pcs   purity 45%
schritte.text: The bag holds stacks. The same ore in the same state goes together: raw copper and smelted copper are two stacks.
On the Bag page, right-click a stack. Then you see what works with it right now.
Selling works without code too: the button at the top right turns the whole bag into money.
In a program you have three options: everything, only one kind, or exactly that many pieces.

schritte.punkt: At the end of the round
schritte.text: Once the round is over the bag is sold anyway. Whatever you processed by then counts towards it.

seiten.kurz: Preparation, run, summary - and round again.

schritte.text: Here the world stands still: nothing is mined, nothing regrows. You buy in the skill tree, write code, look in the bag. Time does not matter.
Now the clock runs, and everything runs with it: your program, mining, regrowing, processing. A round lasts 15 minutes.

During the run you can stop the whole game with F9, or with the button at the bottom right. The clock, the block, a running job and your program all stand still, and go on exactly where they stopped. Careful: the pause at the console is a different one - it only stops your program while the clock keeps running.
When time is up your program is stopped, the running job cancelled and the bag sold. You see what the round brought in.
After that the next preparation begins. Money, skill tree and code stay with you - only the bag is empty.

schritte.code:
Preparation   ->   Run   ->   Summary
     ^
     here you may click the block
schritte.markiere: here you may click the block
schritte.text: During preparation you may click the block by hand. At the very beginning you have neither a program nor money - the first block has to come that way.

seiten.kurz: Here you unlock C++ piece by piece.

schritte.text: At the start you are not allowed to write this line. Every command has to be bought in the skill tree first.

schritte.code: click a card   ->   double click   ->   bought
schritte.text: On the Skills page you see cards. A double-click buys - if you have enough money.
After every purchase new cards appear. What lies behind them is only rolled when you buy: you always see just one step ahead.

schritte.code:
if bought           ->   1 condition allowed
condition+ on top   ->   2 conditions allowed
schritte.text: Whoever buys if may write exactly one if. More comes from the plus cards: +1 condition, +1 loop, +1 console.

schritte.code: Wiki   ->   Functions   ->   only what you already have
schritte.text: Here too only the commands you have already bought are listed. Every new card brings new wiki pages with it.
